messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Walter is a 73-year-old journalist who came to treatment decades into a career built on going toward catastrophe, yet he speaks about one assignment as if it never ended. He had been covering a man-made disaster when the scene turned suddenly chaotic and lethal. What has stayed with him most sharply is not a coherent narrative but fragments with the force of the present: press photographs from the aftermath, the metallic-bitter taste that got into his mouth and would not leave, the sickening fact that nothing about the situation had felt predictable from one second to the next. Even now he says the memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to him. At other times it is less disbelief than immediacy; the event replays like film, and when it comes back he feels as though he is there again rather than remembering from a distance.

In the months after, those fragments began attaching themselves to ordinary life. Related photos were especially potent. As a journalist he still works around image archives, newsroom layouts, and screens full of breaking stories, and when an editor drops disaster photos into a draft or he unexpectedly scrolls past an image resembling that assignment, he feels his body lock. He freezes when threatened, unable to move for a few moments, and after that he becomes rigid about where he sits, insisting on a chair with his back to the wall so he can scan the room. Unpredictable situations in the newsroom—sudden changes, unscheduled visitors, a raised voice from the corridor—bring the same shift in him. A particular taste can do it too, abruptly transporting him. On those days he is certain he will not be able to handle thinking about what happened, and the trigger itself seems to confirm his fear that his mind is no longer under his control.

Over time Walter has come to live as if danger announces itself in small signs that others miss. He listens at night for sounds that might mean someone is entering his home. In restaurants, interview settings, even his own office, he notices potential weapons first—letter openers, heavy lamps, the angle of a bottle on a table—and he cannot relax even when he knows, intellectually, that he is in a safe place. That state of watchfulness makes the world feel full of unpredictable situations, so his triggers multiply rather than narrow. A routine assignment can feel loaded because anything might change without warning, and his attention catches on photographs and sensory details before he is aware he is searching for them. When he is this keyed up, the old film starts running again. A creak in his apartment or the sight of an object that could be used as a weapon is enough to pull him back into the event, and afterward he takes it as further proof that something in him has been permanently altered.

What frightens Walter most is not only the memory itself but what he has come to believe it means. He says that if he lets himself think about the disaster directly, he will not be able to handle it. He has come to believe he will never feel normal emotions again, and that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. Those convictions shape what he does every day. He avoids letting his mind settle, buys things impulsively online and in stores for a brief sense of comfort or distraction, and arranges himself physically against walls and exits as if vigilance were the only thing holding him together. Yet the relief is short-lived. The spending leaves him ashamed and emptier; the constant positioning and scanning tell him the threat must be real; the effort not to think about the event only seems to make the memory more intrusive and unreal at the same time. He says it is like trying not to touch a bruise and ending up pressing on it all day.

The loop has tightened over the last year. Because he freezes when startled and spends so much energy monitoring his surroundings, he is less able to stay present during interviews and has pulled back from some assignments that once gave his life structure. At home he sits in restaurants only if he can face the door, and if he cannot, he leaves. In the office he dreads the image desk, yet when a photo catches him off guard the memory floods back so vividly that the rest of the day is organized around managing it. Each recurrence deepens his conviction that he is damaged beyond repair, and that belief makes him clamp down harder, watch harder, avoid more. He finally sought help after realizing that he no longer recognized his own life as meaningful and was spending nights listening for intruders while old scenes replayed in his head. What he wants, cautiously, is not to erase the event but to stop living as though it is still happening; what he fears is that if he stops guarding against it, he will disappear into it completely.
